---
title: "Forward Contracts: Futures and Forwards — Oral Review"
---

## 🎭 Setting the Scene

A farmer sows wheat in March and trembles at the thought that the price may collapse in September.
Solution: he calls his banker and says "I sell at 200 €/tonne in 6 months, whatever happens".
Contract signed. Irrevocable agreement. No one can back out.
This is a **forward**: firm commitment on both sides, no premium, no emergency exit.
The **futures** is the same thing but in industrial version: standardized, exchange-traded, with a controller (the clearing house) who watches everyone every evening.

---

## 🧠 Chapter's Central Idea

- Fix today the **price of a future transaction** → eliminates price uncertainty.
- Unlike options: **obligation** of both parties (no premium, no choice at maturity).
- The **fair price** of a futures = replication cost = spot price *carried through time* at the risk-free rate.
- The **value** of an already open contract = latent gain/loss discounted.
- The **margin mechanism** eliminates counterparty risk in futures (daily, *marking to market*).
- The term structure can be in **contango** or **backwardation**, but always converges to spot at maturity.

---

## ⚡ Concepts to Be Able to Explain Orally

| Concept | 1-sentence oral explanation | Intuition |
|---|---|---|
| **Forward** | OTC tailor-made contract: buy/sell at $T$ at price $K$, irrevocable. | Farmer who sells his harvest before reaping it. |
| **Futures** | Same principle but standardized, exchange-traded, settled every evening. | Industrial version of the forward, more liquid. |
| **Roll-over** | Close the contract before maturity and open a new, more distant one. | Stay exposed to gold without ever receiving bars. |
| **Initial margin** | Collateral deposited at opening, fraction of the total contract value. | Proof of solvency, not the price of the contract. |
| **Maintenance margin** | Floor threshold below which a margin call is triggered. | Account alarm level. |
| **Margin call** | Replenish the account up to the *initial* margin (not just maintenance). | We reset the counters to zero, not to halfway. |
| **Futures price $F_t$** | Current market delivery price, determined by no-arbitrage. | Spot + financing cost until $T$. |
| **Futures value $f_t$** | Latent gain/loss of an already open contract relative to the initial $K$. | Worth 0 at opening, then evolves. |
| **Contango** | $F_t >$ expected spot: upward-sloping curve with maturity. | Market anticipates rise or high carrying cost. |
| **Backwardation** | $F_t <$ expected spot: downward-sloping curve with maturity. | Strong immediate demand, high *convenience yield*. |

---

## 🔗 Concept Mind Map

- Forward contract → **obligation** (≠ option = right)
- Forward (OTC) → high counterparty risk
- Futures (exchange) → clearing house → near-zero risk
- Futures → daily settlement (*marking to market*) → requires **margin** system
- Initial margin → threshold = maintenance margin → exceeded → **margin call** → replenishment to initial margin
- Spot price $S_t$ + rate $r$ + maturity $T$ → **futures price** $F_t$ by no-arbitrage
- Discrete income $I$ or continuous yield $q$ → **adjustment** of $F_t$
- Current $F_t$ vs initial $K$ → **value** $f_t$ (discounted)
- $F_t$ vs $E[S_T]$ → **contango** or **backwardation**
- Approach of $T$ → $F_t \to S_T$ (**universal convergence**)

---

## 📐 Essential Formulas

| Formula | Meaning | To remember |
|---|---|---|
| $F_t = S_t \cdot e^{r(T-t)}$ | Futures price with no income or cost | Base: spot + financing |
| $F_t = (S_t - I) \cdot e^{r(T-t)}$ | With discrete income $I$ (discounted dividend) | $I$ reduces $F_t$ |
| $F_t = S_t \cdot e^{(r-q)(T-t)}$ | With continuous yield/cost $q$ | $q>0$ income → $F_t$ ↓ ; $q<0$ storage cost → $F_t$ ↑ |
| $f_t = (F_t - K) \cdot e^{-r(T-t)}$ | Value of an existing contract | Discount the expected gain/loss |
| $f_t = S_t - K \cdot e^{-r(T-t)}$ | Simplified value (no dividend) | $f_0 = 0$ always at opening |
| Daily gain $= \Delta F_t \times$ size | Daily *marking to market* | Basis of the margin mechanism |

---

## ⚠️ Classic Pitfalls

- **Futures ≠ Options**: no premium, no choice — firm obligation on both sides.
- **Margin call** → replenishment up to the **initial** margin, not just up to maintenance.
- **$q$ represents income** → $F_t$ decreases; **$q$ represents storage cost** → $F_t$ increases. Do not confuse the sign.
- **$f_0 = 0$ at opening**: no premium exchanged, $K = F_0$ by construction.
- **$F_t \ne$ value $f_t$**: $F_t$ is the market price today; $f_t$ is the economic value of a contract already open with strike $K$ fixed in the past.
- **Convergence at maturity**: $F_T = S_T$ always, whether in contango or backwardation.
- **Forward OTC ≠ Futures**: the forward settles only at maturity; the futures settles every day.

---

## 🎤 Likely Oral Exam Questions

**Q:** What is the fundamental difference between a futures and an option?

**Short answer:** The futures is a bilateral **obligation**; the option is a **right** (buyer only). No premium in a futures.

---

**Q:** Why is the price of a futures $S_t \cdot e^{r(T-t)}$ and not simply $S_t$?

**Short answer:** Because holding the underlying until $T$ costs the **financing** of the position. If that were not the case, there would be an arbitrage opportunity.

---

**Q:** Explain the arbitrage argument if $F_t > S_t \cdot e^{r(T-t)}$.

**Short answer:** Borrow $S_t$, buy spot, short the futures → at maturity, deliver and repay → risk-free profit. Selling pressure brings $F_t$ back to its equilibrium value.

---

**Q:** What is the purpose of the margin mechanism?

**Short answer:** Eliminate counterparty risk by materializing gains and losses every day. If an investor can no longer pay, they are liquidated before the loss becomes irrecoverable.

---

**Q:** What is the value of a futures at opening? Why?

**Short answer:** $f_0 = 0$. At opening, $K = F_0$, so the latent gain is zero: neither party has an advantage over the other.

---

**Q:** What is contango? And backwardation?

**Short answer:** Contango: $F_t >$ expected spot (upward-sloping curve). Backwardation: $F_t <$ expected spot (downward-sloping curve). In both cases, $F_T \to S_T$ at maturity.

---

**Q:** How can an investor stay exposed to a commodity indefinitely without ever receiving it physically?

**Short answer:** Via **roll-over**: close the contract before maturity and reopen a more distant contract on the same delivery.

---

**Q:** What is the impact of a dividend on the price of a futures?

**Short answer:** The discounted dividend $I$ **reduces** $F_t$: holding the asset directly provides an advantage (dividend) that the futures does not provide → $F_t = (S_t - I) \cdot e^{r(T-t)}$.

---

## 🚀 Key Takeaways in 30 Seconds

- **Obligation** firm on both sides (≠ option).
- Futures = Forward but standardized, listed, settled **daily**.
- Daily settlement → **margins** (initial, maintenance, call).
- Margin call → replenishment to **initial** margin.
- Price: $F_t = S_t \cdot e^{r(T-t)}$ — adjust with $I$ (discrete) or $q$ (continuous).
- Value: $f_t = S_t - K \cdot e^{-r(T-t)}$ — worth **0 at opening**.
- Contango: $F_t >$ expected spot. Backwardation: $F_t <$ expected spot.
- **Universal convergence**: $F_T = S_T$ always.
